title: Practice traditions, closed
hookLine: chant, bow, retreat, pilgrimage, perfections, vows

cards: Lay these past weeks out on a table like objects from a long trip. A chant sheet in Pali. A page of the Heart Sutra, marked for a wooden drum.
The mani, sung. The name of Amitabha, walked around a hall. A bow, from a small nod to the full length of the floor.

A long retreat in noble silence, and a sesshin with sore legs and tea at the end. A map of pilgrim roads: Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, Sarnath, Kushinagar, the island of temples, the mountain. The perfections, one a day.
Moon days. Vows for others. A funeral chant, a memorial altar, a meal chant, and yesterday's plan.

teach.b: The tradition has a word for all of this: bhavana. It's often translated meditation, but it's wider than sitting. It means cultivation, bringing something into being, the way a gardener brings up a plant.
Chanting is bhavana. So is bowing, giving, keeping a precept on a moon day. Every practice here is a different kind of gardening.

Why one and not all? The Dhammapada has a picture for how good grows, in Max Müller's words: "Even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled." The verse is about not thinking little of small good acts.
A drop doesn't fill a pot.
A drop, again and again, does. A month of tasting is a sampler. One practice, kept, fills the pot.
Some teachers put it simply: start with what you'll actually do. Not the most impressive practice; the one that fits your mornings, your body, your house.
A short chant you can say while the kettle boils may grow further than a ten-day retreat you never book.

And the schools don't ask you to pick a team. These weeks, a Theravada chant sat next to a Zen drum and a Pure Land name, each taught on its own terms. Choosing one to deepen isn't a verdict on the others.
It's just where your water-drops land for now. And from tomorrow, the festival year comes round again, starting with the full moon of Vesak.

how: Buddhists in different schools keep practices such as chanting, bowing, meditation retreats, pilgrimage, the perfections and vows, and some settle on one or two that they keep daily, often with a teacher's guidance.

o: the most impressive one, even if it doesn't fit your life.
the one you'll actually do, in your real mornings.
all of them at once, so nothing is lost.
games.why: start with what you'll do. in the verse, it's the small drop, again and again, that fills the pot.

practice: Let the practices pass slowly through your mind: the chant, the bow, the retreat, the pilgrim road, the perfections, the vows.

Don't decide with your head; notice which one your attention leans toward, the way a plant leans toward a window, and when one stays, picture doing it tomorrow for a few minutes, in your real kitchen or your real chair.
If more than one comes, keep the first.
